topic.examWeightHint: Unit 2 is one hour and fifty marks, six questions, sat every Summer. Average speed has appeared as the second part of the opening question (Summer 2024 Q1(ii), 2 marks) and as the follow-up to a velocity in a vector question (Summer 2019 Q2(ii)). mustMemorise: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time

Speed is the magnitude of velocity, so it is never negative
Every waiting second belongs in the total time

sheet.howExamined: Unit 2, one hour, fifty marks, six questions, calculator allowed. Average speed comes up as a one to three mark part, usually after a graph or a vector calculation. Summer 2024 Q1 ran draw a displacement/time graph (2) then calculate the average speed (2), with the scheme awarding MW1 for a correct total distance and W1 for the total time and the division. Summer 2019 Q2 asked for a velocity and then for the speed that went with it. Schemes are written in MW and W.
traps: Averaging the stage speeds instead of dividing the total distance by the total time (Summer 2024 Q1)
Leaving the stationary time out of the total time
Handing in the average speed where the average velocity was asked for, or the reverse (Summer 2019 Q2)
Dropping the minus sign from an average velocity
Dividing by one stage's time rather than the whole journey's (Summer 2023 Q6)
Mixing kilometres with seconds, or minutes with metres, in the same fraction
Treating the displacement of a there-and-back journey as anything other than zero

noteBlocks.md: Follow the picture and two different totals come out of it. The bike covers $180 + 240 = 420$ m of road: that is the **distance**. It finishes 60 m past the depot on the far side, so its **displacement** is $-60$ m. Same journey, two honest answers to two different questions.

noteBlocks.prompt: Work out the total distance the bike covers, in metres.
noteBlocks.explain: 180 m out and 240 m back: $180 + 240 = 420$ m of road covered.

noteBlocks.alt: A table of four words: distance is every metre covered so it only grows; displacement is where it ended up with its sign; average speed is total distance divided by total time; average velocity is total displacement divided by total time.

noteBlocks.md:
**Average speed** $= \dfrac{\text{total distance}}{\text{total time}}$ and **average velocity** $= \dfrac{\text{total displacement}}{\text{total time}}$.

The bike takes $40 + 20 + 60 = 120$ s, so its average speed is $420 \div 120 = 3.5$ m/s and its average velocity is $-60 \div 120 = -0.5$ m/s. One journey, one clock, two answers that are not even the same sign.

noteBlocks.prompt: Work out the average velocity of the bike, in m/s.
noteBlocks.explain: Displacement $-60$ m over 120 s gives $-0.5$ m/s. The minus sign says it ended up on the far side of the depot.

noteBlocks.md: The time underneath is the whole journey, from the first second to the last. Waiting counts, because the bike really did take 120 seconds to do what it did. Leaving the stop out would describe a journey that never happened, and it always makes the answer too big.

noteBlocks.title: What an average speed is really saying
noteBlocks.md: It answers one question: if the whole journey had been done at a single steady speed, what would that speed have been? Every second between the start and the finish belongs underneath, whether the body was moving or not.

noteBlocks.explain: $240 + 60 + 300 = 600$ s. Using 540 s would leave the wait out and make the average speed too big.

noteBlocks.md:
**Distance:** $900 + 900 = 1800$ m, because the ferry really did cross twice.
**Time:** $150 + 30 + 180 = 360$ s, the wait included.
**Average speed:** $1800 \div 360 = 5$ m/s.
**Displacement:** the ferry finishes where it began, so it is $0$ m, and the average velocity is $0 \div 360 = 0$ m/s.

noteBlocks.prompt: A swimmer swims six lengths of a straight 25 m pool in 250 s. What is her average speed, in m/s?
noteBlocks.explain: Six lengths is $6 \times 25 = 150$ m, and $150 \div 250 = 0.6$ m/s. Her average velocity is 0, because she finishes at the end she started from.

noteBlocks.title: Speed, Distance and Time
noteBlocks.why: The arithmetic underneath, done slowly. Watch how the units are fixed before the division rather than after it.

noteBlocks.md: A cyclist rides 400 m at 8 m/s and then 400 m at 4 m/s. It is very tempting to write 6 m/s.

noteBlocks.prompt: You have two minutes left and a two-mark average-speed part. What do you write first?
options: The total distance and the total time, on two lines
noteBlocks.answer: The total distance and the total time, on two lines
noteBlocks.explain: Those two lines carry the method mark even if the division then goes wrong, and an unsupported answer earns nothing in Further Mathematics.

noteBlocks.md: It is not 6. The first stretch takes 50 s and the second takes 100 s, so she spends twice as long going slowly. Her average speed is $800 \div 150$, about $5.33$ m/s. Averaging two speeds is safe only when the stages take the same time, so work from the totals every time.

noteBlocks.prompt: A lorry drives 2400 m in 240 s, stops for 60 s, then drives 1500 m in 300 s. What is its average speed?
noteBlocks.explain: 3900 m over 600 s. The 7.5 comes from averaging 10 and 5; the 7.22 comes from leaving the 60-second stop out of the time.

noteBlocks.md:
If the answer line prints m/s, every length must be in metres and every time in seconds before anything is divided. Kilometres with seconds gives a number a thousand times too small.

The first two rows are the ones FM2 asks for.

noteBlocks.title: km/h is not FM2 content
noteBlocks.md: The last two rows are useful, not examined. The letters km appear nowhere in the FM2 papers from 2018 to 2026, and the specification has no unit-conversion statement: m/s to km/h is a GCSE Mathematics skill. Metres and seconds are the units of this unit.

A tram runs along a straight track. It travels 1.8 km in one direction in 200 seconds, then reverses and travels 0.6 km back along the same track in 100 seconds.

(i) Calculate the average speed of the tram, in m/s.
(ii) Calculate the average velocity of the tram, in m/s.

steps.decision: The answer is wanted in metres per second, so put every length into metres before anything else. Mixing kilometres with seconds gives a number a thousand times too small.

steps.working: Total distance $= 1800 + 600 = 2400$ m; total time $= 200 + 100 = 300$ s
steps.decision: Distance adds both legs as lengths. The tram was moving for the whole 300 seconds, so there is no waiting time to include.
Displacement takes the direction into account, so the return leg is subtracted. The tram ends 1200 m along the track from where it set off.
Same time underneath, different quantity on top. The average velocity is half the average speed here, and that gap is the reversal.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: how many metres are there in 1.5 km?

options.feedback: One kilometre is 1000 m, so $1.5 \times 1000 = 1500$ m.
That multiplies by 100. A kilometre is a thousand metres, not a hundred.
That is ten times too many: $1.5 \times 1000$, not $1.5 \times 10000$.
That divides by 1000, which turns kilometres into something a thousand times smaller than a metre.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: how many seconds are there in 5 minutes?

options.feedback: One minute is 60 s, so $5 \times 60 = 300$ s.
That multiplies by 100. A minute is 60 seconds.
That is 5 minutes written as a fraction of an hour, which is not what the question asked for.
That is one minute. There are five of them.

items.skill: Prerequisite: speed from a distance and a time

options.text: 5 m/s
options.feedback: $150 \div 30 = 5$ m/s: metres on top, seconds underneath.
The fraction is upside down. Speed is distance divided by time.
Multiplying gives neither a speed nor anything else useful here. Divide instead.
Subtracting does not give a rate. Speed is a division.

items.stem: How is the average speed of a journey worked out?
items.skill: State the rule for average speed

options.text: Total distance divided by total time
options.feedback: One distance, one time, one division, whatever happened in between.

options.text: The mean of the speeds of the separate stages
options.feedback: That only agrees when the stages take equal times. The Summer 2024 examiners reported that only the stronger candidates used total distance over total time.

options.text: Total displacement divided by total time
options.feedback: That is the average velocity. For a journey that turns back, the two answers differ.

options.text: Total time divided by total distance
options.feedback: Upside down: that gives seconds per metre. Speed is metres per second.

items.stem: A runner runs 600 m along a straight track and then runs the same 600 m back, taking 300 seconds altogether. What is her average velocity?
items.skill: Average velocity of a journey that returns to its start

options.text: 0 m/s
options.feedback: She finishes where she started, so her displacement is zero and so is her average velocity. Her average speed is 4 m/s.

options.text: 4 m/s
options.feedback: That is her average speed, from 1200 m over 300 s. Velocity uses the displacement, which is zero here.

options.text: 2 m/s
options.feedback: That divides one leg of 600 m by the whole 300 s. Average velocity uses the displacement for the whole journey, which is zero.
That is a distance, not a rate. A velocity always has a time underneath it.

items.stem: A cyclist rides 400 m at 8 m/s and then a further 400 m at 4 m/s. Is her average speed for the 800 m equal to 6 m/s?
items.skill: Reject the mean of two speeds

options.text: No, because she spends longer on the slower stretch
options.feedback: 50 s then 100 s, so 800 m in 150 s, which is about 5.33 m/s. The slow stretch weighs more because it lasts longer.

options.text: Yes, because the two distances are the same
options.feedback: Equal distances do not make equal times. Averaging speeds is only safe when the times match.

options.text: Yes, because 8 and 4 have a mean of 6
options.feedback: The mean of the two speeds is not the average speed. Work out the total distance and the total time instead.

options.text: No, because average speed uses the displacement
options.feedback: The verdict is right but the reason is not: average speed uses the total distance. Displacement belongs to average velocity.

items.stem: Which of these can be negative?
items.skill: Decide which quantity can be negative

options.text: Average velocity, because it carries a direction
options.feedback: Velocity and displacement are vectors, so they carry a sign. Speed and distance are sizes and never do.

options.text: Average speed, because a body can go backwards
options.feedback: Going backwards makes the velocity negative. The speed is the size of it, so it stays positive.

options.text: Total distance, when the body returns
options.feedback: Distance keeps counting upwards whichever way the body moves. The displacement is the one that can fall.

options.text: None of them, because time cannot be negative
options.feedback: Time being positive says nothing about the top of the fraction. A displacement of -60 m over 120 s gives -0.5 m/s.

items.stem: A van drives for 240 s, waits for 60 s and drives on for 300 s. What time goes underneath in its average speed?

options.text: 600 s, the whole journey including the wait
options.feedback: Average speed covers the journey as it happened, and the van really did take 600 s.

options.text: 540 s, the time it was moving
options.feedback: Leaving the wait out gives the average speed while moving, which is a different quantity and always larger.

options.text: 300 s, the longest stage
options.feedback: One stage cannot stand for the whole journey. Add all three times.

options.text: 60 s, the time at rest
options.feedback: That is the wait on its own. The total time is 240 + 60 + 300.

parts.stem:
A gritter lorry leaves its depot and travels 2400 m along a straight road, taking 240 seconds.
It stops for 60 seconds.
It then turns and travels 1500 m back along the same road, taking 300 seconds.

Calculate the total distance travelled by the lorry.

Answer ________ m
hints: Both legs count, whichever way the lorry is pointing.

commonErrors.feedback: That is how far the lorry ends up from the depot, which is its displacement. Distance counts the 1500 m of the return leg as well.

parts.stem:
Calculate the average speed of the lorry for the whole journey.

Answer ________ m/s
hints: The 60 seconds at rest belong in the total time.
Total distance divided by total time.
parts.workedSolution: Total time $= 240 + 60 + 300 = 600$ s, so the average speed is $\dfrac{3900}{600} = 6.5$ m/s.

commonErrors.feedback: The stage speeds are 10 m/s and 5 m/s, and their mean is 7.5 m/s. The mean of two speeds is not an average speed unless the stages take the same time, and here they take 240 s and 300 s. Total distance over total time gives 6.5 m/s.
The total distance is right, so the method mark (M) is safe. The 60 seconds at rest are part of the journey, so the total time is 600 s and not 540 s.

parts.stem:
Calculate the average velocity of the lorry for the whole journey.

Answer ________ m/s
hints: Where does the lorry finish, compared with the depot?
2400 m out and 1500 m back leaves it 900 m from the depot.
parts.workedSolution: Displacement $= 2400 - 1500 = 900$ m, so the average velocity is $\dfrac{900}{600} = 1.5$ m/s.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the average speed again. Average velocity puts the displacement of 900 m on top, not the 3900 m of road covered.

context.setting: A cable car running out and back along a straight cable

parts.stem:
A cable car runs along a straight cable between two stations, P and Q, which are 1.2 km apart.
It travels from P to Q in 150 seconds, waits at Q for 60 seconds, and returns to P in 190 seconds.

Calculate the speed of the cable car on the journey from P to Q, in m/s.

Answer ________ m/s
hints: That leg took 150 s on its own.
parts.workedSolution: $1.2$ km $= 1200$ m, so the speed from P to Q is $\dfrac{1200}{150} = 8$ m/s.

commonErrors.feedback: The 1200 m is right, which is the method mark (M). This part asks about one leg, so divide by the 150 s that leg took rather than by the 400 s of the whole journey.

parts.stem:
Calculate the average speed of the cable car for the whole journey, in m/s.

Answer ________ m/s
hints: The cable car covers 1200 m twice.
The 60 seconds at Q are part of the journey.
parts.workedSolution: Total distance $= 1200 + 1200 = 2400$ m and total time $= 150 + 60 + 190 = 400$ s, so the average speed is $\dfrac{2400}{400} = 6$ m/s.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the mean of the two leg speeds, 8 m/s and about 6.32 m/s. The legs take different times, so their speeds cannot simply be averaged. Use 2400 m over 400 s.
The 2400 m earns the method mark (M). The wait at Q counts, so the time underneath is 400 s rather than 340 s.

parts.stem:
Write down the average velocity of the cable car for the whole journey.

Answer ________ m/s
hints: Where does the cable car finish?
parts.workedSolution: The cable car ends back at P, so its displacement for the whole journey is 0 m and its average velocity is $0$ m/s.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the average speed from the part above. The cable car finishes where it started, so its displacement is zero and so is its average velocity.

questions.solutionProgram: PQ = 1200 m; out 150 s, wait 60 s, back 190 s; speed out = 1200/150; average speed = 2400/400; average velocity = 0/400

findTheMistake.stem: Cormac is finding the average speed of the gritter lorry. It travels 2400 m in 240 s, stops for 60 s, then travels 1500 m back in 300 s. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 3 takes the mean of the two stage speeds. That would only be right if the lorry spent the same time on each stage, and it does not: 240 seconds out against 300 seconds back, with a 60-second stop in between that is not counted at all. Average speed has one definition, and it is total distance divided by total time.
findTheMistake.feedback: Both stage speeds are correct, and they would earn their marks in a part that asked for them. This part asks for an average speed, and the mean of two speeds is a different quantity: it earns no method mark because the method itself is not the one the scheme rewards. The Summer 2024 examiners called this part surprisingly poorly answered and said only the stronger candidates used total distance over total time.

prompts.prompt: Write the rule for average speed.
prompts.answer: Average speed = total distance divided by total time, with every stage of the journey counted, waiting included.

prompts.prompt: Write the rule for average velocity.
prompts.answer: Average velocity = total displacement divided by total time. The displacement carries a sign.

prompts.prompt: Why is the average speed of a journey not the mean of the stage speeds?
prompts.answer: Because the stages usually last different times, and the longer stage counts for more. The mean is only right when the times are equal.

prompts.prompt: A body returns to where it began. What is its average velocity?
prompts.answer: Zero, because its displacement is zero, however fast it was moving.

prompts.prompt: How are speed and velocity related?
prompts.answer: Speed is the magnitude of velocity: the same size, without the direction. Speed is never negative.

prompts.prompt: How do you change a speed in km/h into m/s?
prompts.answer: Divide by 3.6, or change the kilometres into metres and the hour into 3600 seconds.

prompts.prompt: A journey includes a stop. Does the stopped time go into the average speed?
prompts.answer: Yes. The total time is the whole journey from start to finish, including every wait.
